source_text: Οὐ μὴν οὐδὲ μακαριότης ψυχῆς κεχωρισμένης σώματος· οὐδὲ γὰρ τὴν θατέρου τούτων ἐξ ὧν συνέστηκεν ἄνθρωπος ἐσκοποῦμεν ζωὴν ἢ τέλος, ἀλλὰ τοῦ συνεστῶτος ἐξ ἀμφοῖν· τοιοῦτος γὰρ πᾶς ὁ τόνδε τὸν βίον λαχὼν ἄνθρωπος, καὶ δεῖ τῆς τούτου ζωῆς εἶναί τι τέλος οἰκεῖον. Εἰ δὲ τοῦ συναμφοτέρου τὸ τέλος, τοῦτο δὲ οὔτε ζώντων αὐτῶν ἔτι κατὰ τόνδε τὸν βίον εὑρεθῆναι δυνατὸν διὰ τὰς πολλάκις ἤδη ῥηθείσας αἰτίας, οὔτε μὴν ἐν χωρισμῷ τυγχανούσης τῆς ψυχῆς, τῷ μηδὲ συνεστάναι τὸν τοιοῦτον ἄνθρωπον διαλυθέντος ἢ καὶ πάντη σκεδασθέντος τοῦ σώματος, κἂν ἡ ψυχὴ διαμένῃ καθ᾿ ἑαυτήν, ἀνάγκη πᾶσα κατ᾿ ἄλλην τινὰ τοῦ συναμφοτέρου καὶ τοῦ αὐτοῦ ζώου σύστασιν τὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων φανῆναι τέλος. Τούτου δ᾿ ἐξ ἀνάγκης ἑπομένου, δεῖ πάντως γενέσθαι τῶν νεκρωθέντων ἢ καὶ πάντη διαλυθέντων σωμάτων ἀνάστασιν καὶ τοὺς αὐτοὺς ἀνθρώπους συστῆναι πάλιν· ἐπειδή γε τὸ μὲν τέλος οὐχ ἁπλῶς, οὐδὲ τῶν ἐπιτυχόντων ἀνθρώπων, ὁ τῆς φύσεως τίθεται νόμος, ἀλλ᾿ αὐτῶν ἐκείνων τῶν κατὰ τὴν προλαβοῦσαν ζωὴν βεβιωκότων, τοὺς δ᾿ αὐτοὺς ἀνθρώπους συστῆναι πάλιν ἀμήχανον, μὴ τῶν αὐτῶν σωμάτων ταῖς αὐταῖς ψυχαῖς ἀποδοθέντων. Τὸ δ᾿ αὐτὸ σῶμα τὴν αὐτὴν ψυχὴν ἀπολαβεῖν ἄλλως μὲν ἀδύνατον, κατὰ μόνην δὲ τὴν ἀνάστασιν δυνατόν· ταύτης γὰρ γενομένης καὶ τὸ τῇ φύσει τῶν ἀνθρώπων πρόσφορον ἐπακολουθεῖ τέλος. Τέλος δὲ ζωῆς ἔμφρονος καὶ λογικῆς κρίσεως οὐκ ἂν ἁμάρτοι τις εἰπὼν τὸ τούτοις ἀπερισπάστως συνδιαιωνίζειν οἷς μάλιστα καὶ πρώτως ὁ φυσικὸς συνήρμοσται λόγος, τῇ τε θεωρίᾳ τοῦ ὄντος καὶ τῶν ἐκείνῳ δεδογμένων ἀπαύστως ἐπαγάλλεσθαι· κἂν οἱ πολλοὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐμπαθέστερον καὶ σφοδρότερον τοῖς τῇδε προσπεπονθότες ἄστοχοι τούτου διατελῶσιν. Οὐ γὰρ ἀκυροῖ τὴν κοινὴν ἀποκλήρωσιν τὸ πλῆθος τῶν ἀποπιπτόντων τοῦ προσήκοντος αὐτοῖς τέλους, ἰδιαζούσης τῆς ἐπὶ τούτοις ἐξετάσεως καὶ τῆς ἑκάστῳ συμμετρουμένης ὑπὲρ τῶν εὖ ἢ κακῶς βεβιωμένων τιμῆς ἢ δίκης.
thought_title: The end belongs to the whole person, so resurrection is necessary
orientation: Athenagoras is concluding his argument that the proper end of human life belongs to the whole person, not to the soul alone, and therefore the resurrection of bodies must occur.
pass_a_gloss: Nor indeed is there blessedness of a soul separated from a body. For we were not considering the life or end of either one of these from which a human being is composed, but of the one composed from both. For every human being who has obtained this life is such, and there must be some proper end of the life of this one. But if the end is of the whole person, and this is not possible to be found while they are still living according to this life because of the causes already often stated, nor indeed while the soul is in separation, because such a human being does not even exist when the body has been dissolved or even completely scattered, even if the soul remains by itself, it is altogether necessary that the end of human beings appear according to some other composition of the whole person and of the same living being. And since this follows of necessity, there must certainly occur a resurrection of the bodies that have died or even been completely dissolved, and the same human beings must be composed again. Since indeed the law of nature sets the end not simply, nor of any chance human beings, but of those very ones who have lived according to the previous life, and it is impossible for the same human beings to be composed again unless the same bodies are given back to the same souls. And for the same body to receive back the same soul is impossible in any other way, but possible only according to the resurrection. For when this has occurred, the end that is fitting to the nature of human beings also follows. And one would not miss the mark in saying that the end of an intelligent and rational life of judgment is to live forever with these things undistractedly, with which especially and primarily the natural reason has been fitted, and to rejoice unceasingly in the contemplation of the one who is and of the things decreed by him. Even if the many among human beings, having been affected more passionately and more violently by the things here, continue to miss this mark. For the multitude of those who fall away from the end that is proper to them does not invalidate the common allotment, since the examination concerning these things is particular, and the honor or punishment measured out to each one for the things lived well or badly.

pass_b_english: Nor is the blessedness of a soul separated from its body the point at issue. We were not examining the life or end of one of the two parts from which a human being is composed, but of the being composed of both. For every human being who has obtained this present life is such a being, and there must be some end proper to his life. If the end belongs to the whole person, and this end cannot be found while they are still living this present life, for the reasons already stated many times, nor while the soul exists in separation—since such a human being no longer exists once the body has been dissolved or entirely scattered, even if the soul remains by itself—then it is absolutely necessary that the end of human beings appear in some other composition of the whole person and of the same living being. Since this follows by necessity, there must certainly be a resurrection of bodies that have died or been entirely dissolved, and the same human beings must be composed again. For the law of nature sets the end not simply, nor for just any human beings, but for those very persons who lived the previous life; and it is impossible for the same human beings to be composed again unless the same bodies are given back to the same souls. For the same body to receive back the same soul is impossible in any other way, but possible only through the resurrection. When this takes place, the end proper to human nature follows as well. As for the end of an intelligent and rational life, one would not be wrong to say that it is to abide undistractedly with those things to which the natural reason is chiefly and primarily fitted, and to rejoice unceasingly in the contemplation of the One who is and of what he has decreed—even if the majority of human beings, having clung too passionately and violently to the things of this world, miss this end. For the multitude of those who fall away from the end proper to them does not nullify the shared allotment, since the examination of these matters is particular, and honor or punishment is measured out to each person for a life lived well or badly.

problems.why: Glossary mandates 'the whole person' for συναμφότερον; missing definite article in 'of the whole person and of the same living being'.
problems.fix: of the whole person and of the same living being

problems.quote: the law of nature does not set the end simply, nor for just any human beings
problems.source_quote: ὁ τῆς φύσεως τίθεται νόμος, ἀλλ᾿ αὐτῶν ἐκείνων τῶν κατὰ τὴν προλαβοῦσαν ζωὴν βεβιωκότων
problems.why: Greek says nature's law 'sets' (τίθεται) the end, not 'does not set'; the negation οὐδὲ goes with 'simply' and 'for just any', but 'does not set' misrepresents the positive verb.
problems.fix: the law of nature sets the end not simply nor for just any human beings, but for those very persons

problems.why: ἀποκλήρωσιν means 'allotment' or 'apportionment', but 'common allotment' obscures that this refers to the shared/standard end appointed for all, not something 'common' in a vulgar sense.

problems.quote: honor or punishment is measured out
problems.source_quote: τῆς ἑκάστῳ συμμετρουμένης ὑπὲρ τῶν εὖ ἢ κακῶς βεβιωμένων τιμῆς ἢ δίκης
problems.why: Missing 'for a life lived well or badly'—the Greek specifies the basis for honor/punishment is how one lived, not just that one lived.
problems.fix: honor or punishment is measured out to each person for a life lived well or badly

edits.old: the law of nature does not set the end simply, nor for just any human beings
edits.new: the law of nature sets the end not simply, nor for just any human beings

fixed: The gloss already contains 'of the whole person and of the same living being' with the definite article, so no change is needed.
The English already says 'honor or punishment is measured out to each person for a life lived well or badly', so no change is needed.

last_rejected.why: Source says 'the being composed of both,' i.e. the whole person; English is awkward and loses the referent.
last_rejected.ruling: English 'being composed of both' accurately renders τοῦ συνεστῶτος ἐξ ἀμφοῖν; slightly awkward but meaning clear.

last_rejected.quote: the One who is and of what he has decreed
last_rejected.source_quote: τοῦ ὄντος καὶ τῶν ἐκεῖνῳ δεδογμένων
last_rejected.why: Source is neuter 'what has been decreed by Him,' not personal 'he has decreed.'
last_rejected.fix: what is, and of what has been decreed by Him
last_rejected.ruling: ἐκείνῳ is masculine dative referring back to τοῦ ὄντος (God); 'he has decreed' correctly interprets the personal referent.

last_rejected.why: Glossary term 'continuance' for διαμονή is not used; 'abide' misses the 'continuance' sense of enduring together.
last_rejected.fix: to continue undistractedly with those things
last_rejected.ruling: συνδιαιωνίζειν means to live/abide together with; 'abide undistractedly' captures this. No glossary term διαμονή appears in source.
